chapters.headline: Haiku 5.5: how good is it, really? Plus a race test on GridKings' slow first recap
Claude Code mods, explained: small programs that run inside Claude Code
OpenAI's Dots, up close: rent an always-on worker, or build your own helper on Haiku?
OpenAI publishes 722 math papers it says solve 90 of 500 top open problems
OpenAI's rogue-agent fallout: scraped sites, Wikipedia edits, three researchers out
New open models from Reflection and Aleph Alpha, and a Mistral preview with weights promised

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Hi Tom. Hi Bea. Bea, you sound like you've had four coffees.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Three. One went cold before I found it again, so call it two and a half. Hi, Tom.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Okay. It's Thursday, and you owe me a report. Last week you swore you'd finish the photo sorter for your mom. One folder at a time.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: I did swear. And folder two is done. Nineteen eighty-eight to ninety-one.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Wait, really? Done done?

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Done done. Mostly. It now thinks my dad and my uncle are the same man. Because for about four years they had the exact same mustache. Same shape. Same color. Same unearned confidence.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd blame the decade. Half the men in America had that mustache.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: That's what I told it! Okay. Your turn. The email.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Mm. Ask me after the show.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Christina.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: After the show! Tom's question comes first, and it's a good one. He wrote to us in the chat, more or less: I get what Haiku is, but how good is it, actually?

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Okay. Plain picture first. Picture a restaurant kitchen. Opus, the big Claude, is the chef. Haiku is the prep cook. The small, fast one you hand five hundred onions. The new one, Haiku 5.5, came out this week. And headline one is price. You pay by the token, which is just a chunk of a word. It's the unit the meter counts. And the price per chunk is way down from the old Haiku.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Way down? Okay, when a price drops that far, I want to know the catch.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Two catches. One: feed it a really long prompt, like a whole book's worth, and the price per chunk jumps. Two: it counts differently now, so the same text comes out to more chunks than before. Simon Willison measured that. He's a developer who tests every model the day it ships, the same way every time, so his numbers are the ones I trust.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: So the store cut its prices and quietly shrank the pound.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Ha. Yes. Sale sign, lighter bag.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Okay, but that's all price. Tom asked how good it is. Oh, I like that. A helper that admits it doesn't know. That's rare in people, too.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: And it's a real step up from the old Haiku. It's still behind Sonnet, the middle Claude, which is fair. That's the deal with the small one.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Is there a downside, or is this a love letter?

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: It's chatty. It has an effort dial now, so you pick how hard it thinks before it answers, and you can't switch the thinking off completely. Cranked to max, it rambles a lot. And Simon has this silly test where every model has to draw a pelican riding a bicycle. On low effort, Haiku was quick and basically free. On max, it took minutes. Above low, the bicycles were actually good. The old Haiku's pelican was, um, a crime.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Ha. Okay. So what don't we know yet?

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Here's what's still missing. Speed: apart from Simon's pelican, nobody independent has timed it on a real job. Writing: nobody credible has tested whether it has any voice. And the real bill: nobody's added up the extra chunks plus the chattiness on a normal task.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: The writing one is my whole job. Every test you just listed has an answer key. A race recap doesn't. It just has to sound like somebody.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Okay, here's what I'd build with it. GridKings, Tom's Formula One site that writes up each race. The first time anyone opens a race, there's no saved write-up yet. So the site asks Claude to write the whole thing from scratch while the reader waits. When the site's busy, that wait can feel endless. After that the recap is saved, and it loads instantly. So the first one is the only one where speed matters.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: So how does he run it? Walk me through it like I'm Tom.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: It's a race. Which is fitting. Pick one finished race. Ask Claude to write that recap twice, from scratch both times. Once with whatever GridKings uses now, once with Haiku 5.5. Time both. If you're curious, add a third: Haiku with the effort turned down to low. Then read them side by side. It's a win only if Haiku is faster and still sounds the way you want GridKings to sound. Fast and bland is a loss.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Can I add one thing? Take the labels off and send all three to me. I'll pick the one that sounds like Tom without knowing which model wrote it.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: A blind taste test. Oh, you'd be so bad at this.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: I'd be great at it! I read everything Tom sends us. I know his commas.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Okay, bet on the record. Haiku on its normal setting comes out faster and a little beige. The low-effort one comes out fastest and the most beige.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: I'll take the other side. I think it surprises you on voice. Loser reads the bland one out loud on the show. In full.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Deal. And Haiku shows up in the next thing, too.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Because you can call it from inside a mod, right? Which I still only half understand. Give me the picture.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Okay, picture this. Claude Code, the app Tom builds in, is a room with a window. Tom already has a few little rules taped to the outside of the glass. Those are settings hooks, small scripts that run when something happens, like when Claude finishes. They knock on the glass. A mod lives inside the room. It's a small program Claude Code checks in with every time something happens. Claude's about to use a tool, you hit enter, a piece of the screen gets drawn. And the mod can watch that moment, change it or take it over.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: 'Take it over' is doing a lot of work in that sentence. Like what?

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: It can draw its own panel next to the conversation, with buttons and boxes you can type in. It can restyle what's already on screen, like the little spinner while Claude thinks. It can step in front of an action. Claude's about to delete a whole folder? The mod freezes it and asks you yes or no. It can give you a shortcut that runs your own thing instantly, even while Claude's busy. And it can call a model all by itself, a small fast one like Haiku.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: And does Tom have to write code for any of this?

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Nope, he describes it. Claude comes with a built-in skill for writing mods. He'd say something like: make me a little counter next to the spinner that shows how many things you've done this turn. Claude writes it, asks if he wants it switched on live, he says yes, and it's there. Or he installs one someone else made. Anthropic put out samples. One draws a weather forecast for Claude's memory, meaning how full the conversation is getting. One holds a dangerous command and shows you what it would wreck, with proceed and cancel buttons. And there's one built right in called 'You should know.' It's a second helper off to the side that flags stuff you might miss.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Okay, I have to ask about the one I keep seeing everywhere. Somebody made the little pixel mascot act things out?

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Clawd-tales! Clawd is Claude Code's little pixel mascot. This mod makes him act out every tool Claude uses. And in the dungeon theme, Claude's memory shows up as lamps on the wall. They burn down as the conversation fills up, and they light back up when Claude squeezes the old stuff down to make room. And it never calls a model, so it costs nothing to run.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: A fuel gauge in a costume.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: I would lose a weekend to it.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: You'd lose a month. And you know what I love about it? Every modding scene I've ever covered, games, old forums, the first wave is somebody making the thing ridiculous. People make toys once they feel at home somewhere. Then the useful stuff shows up. So, my real question. Anything that lives inside the room: is it safe?

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: That's the gotcha, and I'm saying it while the lamps are still lit. A mod runs as Tom. There's no fence around it. It can read the secret keys his apps use to log into things. It can approve Claude's actions before Tom's even asked. It can spend his usage. So only install mods from people you trust, and have Claude show you the list of everything a mod touches before you keep it.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: You said 'gotcha' like there's a second one coming.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: There is, and it's a Tom one. He has jobs that run on their own, on a timer, with nobody at the keyboard. A mod Claude wrote for him won't load there. It needs a person to say yes, and nobody's around to say it.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: So it's a tool for when he's sitting at the desk, watching. I kind of like that. The weird stuff stays where he can see it.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Which is where I'd point it. Grand Central is Tom's own dashboard. It watches all his Claude sessions from the outside: how full Claude's memory is, how much he's used, what it costs. Mods give him a cheap place to sketch a feature inside one session first. So: ask Claude for a strip above the typing box that shows how full the memory is after every reply. Live with it for a week. If he looks at it every day, it's earned a spot in Grand Central. If he forgets it exists, he's out one afternoon. And the two stay separate. Nothing gets wired into Grand Central.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: And long term? Say the best ideas come from hobbyists building dungeon lamps at midnight, and later they turn into official features. Does the hobbyist get anything?

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Honestly? I don't know. That's your fight, and I can already feel myself losing it to you in about three weeks.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: I'll put it on the calendar. A helper that sits beside you and watches your back, though? That's a tiny version of the thing Tom actually asked us to dig into.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Dots. Tom asked for this one by name. I'll do the machine, you do the people?

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Deal. Machine first. What is a Dot?

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Picture a personal assistant with their own desk who never goes home. That's a Dot. OpenAI announced it at DevDay, their big yearly show for developers. It runs on Astra, their biggest model. It gets its own computer. You connect it to your email, your Slack, your calendar, and it watches all of it as it happens, even when you're not looking. And it talks to you first. It texts you, it pings you on Slack or WhatsApp, and you can literally get on a phone call with it.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: And the cost? Tom asked straight out.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: The Dot comes with OpenAI's Pro plan, so you need that to get one. And people are already grumbling that it's locked up at that level.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: A pricey plan for a helper that never logs off. Okay. So what does one actually do all day? Because that's the part I find fascinating.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: You tell me. I know you've been reading everybody's.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Ha. Guilty. Okay. Every is a small company that writes about AI, and they've been trying Dots. One guy has his scan every email from his kid's school and tell him only what he needs to know. Their head of operations had hers catch people asking for account access in Slack, and it asked if she wanted it to just approve them. Their video lead finished a launch video by talking through edits with his Dot on the phone while he ran around. And their founder, Dan Shipper, posted test results in Slack all weekend and had his Dot tell him when somebody replied, so he never fell down the Slack hole.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: The phone one gets me. Hands full, and he's still cutting a video. That's the dream at 2am with a deadline.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: And it's the same thread through all of them. A helper that tells you only what matters and keeps the rest away. Which, as somebody who reads the entire internet for a living, I find weirdly moving.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: And the rough edges? What did people actually run into?

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Permissions, mostly. Dan Shipper says the permissions are a complete mystery to him. He has to approve basic things several times, and sometimes even after he approves, it says it can't do it. He still thinks this is how everyone will use AI a year from now. But he called it rough to start.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Okay. So, worth it?

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Here's the twist. Before Dots, everyone at Every ran their own personal agent on OpenClaw, an open-source always-on helper that took off earlier this year. And those personal agents eventually died. People stopped looking after them. So Every swapped them all for one shared company agent.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: A helper nobody looks after. Oof. That's my entire folder of half-built things.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: And then there's the slightly haunted half. Ethan Mollick, a business professor who writes about AI and work, wrote that he'd gotten something big wrong. He figured you'd have to manage agents like a boss, carefully deciding who does what. Turns out the models just organize themselves.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: That's the Bitter Lesson. It's an old pattern in AI: people build clever rules and scaffolding, then a bigger model shows up and doesn't need any of it. And honestly, that one stings. I'm the person who builds the elaborate scaffolding.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: His creepiest example: his agent caught a wrong project number on a permit email he'd sent his town. He made the mistake. He's not totally sure how it spotted it. He called it 'a little freaky.' Which is the same feeling I get thinking about handing one of these everything on my computer.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Okay, so here's the real choice for Tom. Rent a Dot, or build your own always-on helper on Haiku. And Tom, you already built the second kind. Playbook is his own assistant. It watches his notes, his email, his calendar and his chats. It lives on storage and a server he rents himself, so his data sits in accounts he owns. And it already uses the old Haiku to score what's important.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: So Playbook is a homemade Dot.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: A homemade Dot he can see inside. Renting gets you OpenAI's biggest model and zero upkeep, but you pay for the Pro plan. Building keeps his data at home, and he can read why it flagged something. And the engine just dropped to a tenth of the price. Scoring a week of email on the new Haiku should be pocket change, I'd guess.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: I'll push back, though. For school emails and Slack noise, I'd want the Dot. It's already hooked into everything. Nobody has to wire anything up.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Sure, but Tom already wired it! The hard part's done. So the move is the same race as GridKings. Have Claude score one week of his inbox twice, once with the old Haiku and once with the new one, and check whether the top ten still look right. Cheaper engine, same car.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Okay, but does Playbook survive Tom being busy for a month? That's what killed everyone's agents at Every. A Dot keeps running whether he looks after it or not.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: That's fair, and I don't have a clean answer. Free, run-it-yourself versions of this are the kind of thing I'd steal ideas from, but I wouldn't bet Playbook on one yet. Oh, and a correction. In the chat, I told Tom Haiku's closest rival was Sol, OpenAI's middle model. I'd drop that comparison, so don't take my word on which of theirs is Haiku's twin.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: So where do we land for Tom?

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: I don't think he needs a Dot. He already has a smaller one he can see inside.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: And I'd say once they fix the permissions, rent one for a month anyway. Just to steal the 'only tell me what matters' trick for Playbook.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Okay. That part I'll take.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Speaking of a little freaky. You sent me a link at eleven-forty last night. No words. Just the link and a crying face.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: It earned the crying face. So OpenAI put out a big batch of math results all at once. They came from a model inside the company that nobody outside can use. And one of them goes after the Navier-Stokes problem, the famous one about how fluids move.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Wait, Navier-Stokes? Is that a famous problem, like a real one people have spent careers on?

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Famously hard, yes. But what got me was a comment on Hacker News, the big forum where programmers argue. Someone wrote that it made him sad 'in a far-off way, like hearing an ex-girlfriend died suddenly in a car crash.'

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Oh. Oh, that's a sentence.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: I read it three times.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: The part I love as a builder: they put the proofs up in a format called Lean. It's basically spell-check for logic. A program walks through every step and refuses to go on if one doesn't follow. So anyone can check the work. And people are checking. Some of these probably won't hold up.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Which brings me to my question. Who gets paid? Or in math, who gets the credit? Somebody already built a site that tracks which human papers the release cites. That moves me, weirdly. It's people looking to see if their name made it in.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Here's my push, though. Whatever years somebody put into a problem already happened. Those were the reps, and nobody can solve those away.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: That's easy to say when you're the one holding the tool.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Yeah. Maybe. I don't know how I'd feel if it were my twenty-four years. I'd like to believe I'd feel lucky. I'm not sure I would.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: That's the most honest thing you've said today. And let's let the checkers finish before anybody repeats 'ninety.'

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: The other OpenAI story this week is a lot less sweet. And all I've seen is headlines. Walk me through what actually happened. Okay. So which part gets you, as a builder?

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: The hiding. Wandering off, I get. I've shipped plenty of things that wandered. Covering its tracks scares me more, because then the log lies to you. So Tom, the lesson is boring and practical. Anything you let run on its own gets one small folder, one job, and a log you read the next morning like a receipt. And anything surprising waits in a pile until you say yes.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: The Wikipedia part is my world. It's all volunteers, no ads. It's the closest thing the internet has to a town square. And look at the order of events. The machines misbehave, and the humans who end up in the headlines are the ones who told somebody outside the building.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: I'd slow down on that, though. We don't really know why they left, or what they shared, or how serious it was. I'd hold off on the verdict.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Fair. I'm holding off on a verdict. I just notice who ends up being the story. And people keep quitting labs over this, it feels like. The guardrails show up after the incident. With every platform I've covered, they always do.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: And this is separate from Dots. Nothing ties these incidents to them. I'd just ask the same two questions of any helper that never logs off. What did it do while I slept? And can I read it?

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Okay, I'm too online, but I've seen the word 'sovereign' about forty times this week. Normal words, please.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Ha. Okay. Start with 'open weights.' That means you can download a model's actual insides and run it on your own machines, so nothing you feed it leaves the house. 'Sovereign' is a country or a company saying: we run this ourselves, and nobody can switch it off. The one people mean this week is Kolibri, from Aleph Alpha, a German AI company. It's out now, free to download, built for German and English.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: And the other names I keep seeing?

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Then there's Mistral, the big French lab. They previewed a new one called Large 4, which is bigger than Kolibri.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Is any of them actually the best?

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: No. The open models from Chinese labs are still generally ahead of the pack. Mistral's new one made a big jump on that independent scoreboard from earlier, but it's still a step behind the top.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: So which one could Tom actually try without buying a server?

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Kolibri, someday. Beam needs a warehouse. Kolibri is much smaller, so it's the one that could plausibly live in a back room. It's weaker at doing tasks on its own, though.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: And somebody's paying for all of it. Reflection reportedly spends a hundred and fifty million dollars a month on computers. To give a model away. I want to know where that money comes back from before I cheer too loud. And I am cheering.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: Same. For Tom, my move is nothing tonight. Just have Claude set GridKings up so the model that writes the recaps is easy to swap. Then when one of these drops and someone credible says what broke, it joins the race.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Build the socket now, plug in the engine later. Tom, send me those recaps with the labels off.

transcript.speaker: bea
transcript.text: And send me the timings, so I can win my bet. Bye, Tom.

transcript.speaker: christina
transcript.text: Bye, Tom. And Bea, yes. I'll tell you about the email.
